title: TB3-09044
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) a citizen of Taiwan, appeals the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying her claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) a citizen of Taiwan, appeals the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying her claim for refugee protection. She has tendered new evidence in this appeal and requests an oral hearing if the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) impugns the declarations made in her affidavits. The Appellant asks that the RAD set aside the decision and substitute a determination that she is a Convention refugee or, in the alternative, refer her claim back to the RPD for redetermination.

Pursuant to Section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD that the Appellant is not a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. Her appeal is denied.

The Appellant alleged before the RPD that she fears returning to Taiwan because of the domestic abuse she suffered at the hands of her Taiwanese husband. Her claim for refugee protection was heard by the RPD on October 10, 2013. In a decision of November 20, 2013, the RPD rejected her claim finding that she had state protection in Taiwan. The RPD further found that she had the right of citizenship in the Philippines and that she would also be afforded state protection there.

The Appellant appealed the RPD's decision to the RAD. In the appeal, the Appellant acknowledged that, although she is a Taiwanese national, she is entitled to citizenship in the Philippines. However, she argued that the RPD's finding on state protection in Taiwan and the Philippines was not reasonable. In her appeal, the Appellant tendered a number of documents as new evidence to support her arguments. In a decision dated March 21, 2014, the RAD rejected the admission of the proposed new evidence and rejected the Appellant's appeal finding that the RPD's finding on state protection was reasonable.

The Appellant appealed the RAD's decision to the Federal Court. In a decision dated June 30, 2015, the Federal Court granted the appeal. The Court found that the RAD erred when it applied the reasonableness standard of review to the appeal. The appeal was returned to the RAD for redetermination.

The Appellant has submitted an additional Memorandum of Argument as well as additional documentary documents relative to the issue of state protection in both Taiwan and the Philippines. In the new Memorandum, the Appellant again submits that state protection is not reasonably available to her in her countries of nationality.

Counsel has made submissions in regard to the role that the RAD plays in the review of an RPD decision. However, the RAD finds that the Federal Court decision, in Huruglica,1 provides the RAD with guidance in relation to the appropriate standard that must be applied by a specialized tribunal such as the RAD to decisions of a first-level administrative tribunal. Justice Phelan states in paragraphs 54 and 55 of the foregoing decision: [54] Having concluded that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD's decision on the standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons above, the RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decision. [55] In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on facts only where there is an "overriding and palpable error".

Accordingly, the RAD will conduct its own assessment of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Deference will be afforded to the credibility findings of the RPD or to other findings where the RPD has a particular advantage in reaching its conclusions. ADMISSIBILITY OF NEW EVIDENCE PRESENTED ON APPEAL

As provided for in s. 110(3) of the IRPA, with certain exceptions, the RAD must proceed without a hearing, on the basis of the record of the proceedings of the RPD and may accept documentary evidence and written submissions from the Minister and refugee claimant. Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the person who is the subject of the appeal may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

The Appellant has submitted a number of documents as new evidence relative to domestic violence and state protection with her original Appellant's Record. (a) Three articles which address spousal violence including risk after marital separation;2 (b) Five articles specific to domestic violence in Taiwan;3 (c) Six articles on domestic violence in the Philippines;4 and (d) Five articles about issues related to accessible justice.5

The Appellant also tendered additional documents as new evidence in its additional Memorandum including: (a) Five articles relating specifically to domestic violence in Taiwan;6 and (b) Six articles relating specifically to domestic violence in the Philippines.7

The RAD's analysis of the admissibility of the proposed new evidence must begin first with the test set out in s. 110(4). In assessing whether the proposed new evidence meets the statutory provisions of s. 110(4), the RAD considered the following: (a) First, did the evidence arise after the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim? Here, the RAD may consider whether the evidence is capable of proving the current state of affairs in the country of feared persecution, or an event that occurred, or a circumstance that arose after the rejection of the refugee claim. (b) The RAD will consider not only the date on which the document came into existence but the timing of the event or circumstance which the document seeks to prove. For example, an affidavit or newspaper article may have been created after the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim, but the information in the document may be several years old, and the RAD may therefore find that the evidence did not arise after the rejection of the claim, despite the date of the document. (c) It is important to note here that s. 110(4) does not contemplate whether the evidence arose after the RPD's hearing, but rather after the rejection of the Appellant's claim. Where a document arose after the hearing but before the rejection of the refugee claim, it is necessary for the RAD to consider whether the Appellant could have presented the document to the RPD by way of a post-hearing submission. (d) If the evidence is capable of proving an event that occurred or circumstances that arose after the RPD hearing, then the evidence must be considered, and the RAD will proceed to assess the probative value of the evidence. (e) Second, if the RAD finds that the evidence did not arise after the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim, it must consider the next factor in s. 110(4). If the evidence is capable of proving only an event that occurred or circumstances that arose prior to the rejection, has the Appellant established that the evidence was not reasonably available for presentation to the RPD before it rejected the claim, or that it proves a fact that was unknown to the Appellant at the time of the hearing? If so, the RAD will proceed to assess the probative value of the evidence. (f) Third, if the RAD finds that the evidence did not arise after the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim, and that it was reasonably available at the time of the rejection, it must consider the final part of the s. 110(4) test: could the Appellant reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented the evidence prior to the rejection of the refugee claim? If so, the evidence need not be considered. If the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected to present the evidence to the RPD, the RAD will proceed to assess the probative value of the evidence.

In the case at hand, the Appellant submits that the new evidence meets the test set out in s.110(4) because it arose after the rejection of the claim or that she could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented the evidence prior to the rejection of her refugee claim.

In assessing the Appellant's argument, the RAD has taken into consideration that the Appellant was self-represented at the RPD hearing and had not received assistance in preparing her submissions to the RPD. The RAD accepts that the Appellant had little money to pay for a lawyer or consultant and was unfamiliar with the legal aid process. In addition, the RAD has considered the Appellant's arguments keeping in mind the Gender Guidelines particularly in light of the fact that the Appellant is a victim of domestic violence who was found to be credible by the RPD. The RAD further finds that, given the circumstances in this particular appeal, in order to conduct a full, fact-based appeal, the RAD must show flexibility in order to address the issues on appeal.

Accordingly, the RAD finds that the proposed new evidence does satisfy the statutory requirements of section 110(4) of the IRPA, and, as such, all of the documents tendered in this appeal are admitted as evidence in this appeal.

The Appellant submits that the determinative issue in this appeal is the availability of state protection for her in the Philippines and Taiwan. She argues that the documentary evidence she tendered demonstrates that the RPD's finding on state protection was in error. More specifically, the Appellant argues that the efforts of Taiwanese and Filipino authorities to protect women fleeing long-term spousal abuse have proven ineffective in that the rate of domestic violence in both countries is increasing in recent years.
paragraphs.heading_before: ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE CLAIM

paragraphs.text: The RAD is not persuaded by the Appellant's argument in this regard. While the RAD agrees that the determinative issue in this appeal is state protection in the case of Taiwan, the RAD is not persuaded that state protection is the determinative issue in the case of the Philippines. Since the Appellant has now conceded that she has citizenship rights to two countries,8 the burden is on the Appellant to show a well-founded fear of persecution in both countries of reference. If the RAD finds that she does not have a well-founded fear of persecution in any one of the two countries of reference, the claim for protection does not succeed.

In that regard, the RAD finds that the Appellant has not demonstrated that she has a well-founded fear of persecution in the Philippines. The RAD notes that the only agent of persecution is the Appellant's husband. She argues in her pleadings that she fears he will be able to find her in the Philippines because she will be forced to contact him to secure custody or access to her children. She further argues that, once he knows she is in the Philippines, it will be easy for him to acquire a visa to travel to the Philippines.

However, the Appellant has not tendered any corroborative evidence to support her argument that Taiwanese citizens have easy access to Filipino visas. More importantly, the Appellant has not offered any evidence to establish that her husband has the means or interest in pursuing her outside of Taiwan. The RAD notes there is no evidence that the agent of persecution has ever expressed an interest in pursuing her.

The RAD notes that the Appellant has stated in her pleadings that her husband has not attempted to contact her in Canada because he does not know where she is living currently but that he would come to know where she was living through her efforts to secure custody or visitation with her children. The RAD finds that the Appellant's concern in this regard would be mitigated through the use of a third party such as her family members, a lawyer or a non-government organization (NGO) offering services to abused women in the Philippines.

The RAD also notes that the Appellant has a large extended family in the Philippines, but no evidence has been adduced that her husband has attempted to contact her family there. The RAD finds it reasonable to expect that, if the Appellant's husband was interested in locating her whereabouts, he would make some efforts to contact her family in the Philippines. The RAD notes that it has been two years since the Appellant left Taiwan, yet the Appellant has not adduced any evidence that he has made any efforts to locate her. The absence of any evidence of effort on the part of the agent of persecution to find the Appellant in the Philippines undermines her argument that he would travel there and locate her. The Appellant's belief that he could find her in the Philippines is highly speculative in nature. The RAD finds that, even if the agent of persecution did come to know her location in the Philippines, there is simply insufficient evidence in the record to substantiate her fear that he would travel there to harm her.

In making its determination, the RAD has considered the Chairperson's Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.9 The RAD has also considered the hardships that the Appellant may encounter in returning to the Philippines. The RAD finds the information in the objective evidence reveals that the re-acquisition citizenship in the Philippines is an automatic right afforded by the citizenship act of the Philippines.10 Regardless, as stated previously in these Reasons, the Appellant concedes she has right of citizenship in the Philippines. The RAD further finds that the hardships associated with relocating back to the Philippines would be mitigated by the fact that the majority of the Appellant's siblings and her mother are living in the Philippines. No evidence has been adduced that she is estranged from her family in the Philippines, and it is reasonable to expect that her family would assist her by providing housing and support upon her return.
The RAD finds, on the basis of the foregoing, that there is no more than a mere possibility that the Appellant would be persecuted in the Philippines if she returns. State Protection

In the alternative, if the agent of persecution does manage to locate the Appellant and chooses to travel to the Philippines in order to harm her, the RAD has considered the adequacy of state protection in the Philippines in light of all the evidence.

The Appellant submits that, if she seeks state protection in the Philippines, it would not be reasonably forthcoming. The RAD finds that the Appellant cannot rebut the presumption of state protection in a functioning democracy only with asserting a subjective reluctance to engage the state. Doubting the effectiveness of the protection offered by the state when the Appellants have not really tested it does not rebut the presumption of state protection.

In a functioning democracy, such as in the Philippines where the state is willing and able to provide a measure of protection, failure to pursue protection opportunities will be fatal to the claim unless there is a compelling explanation for the failure, even when those protective services have gaps or deficiencies. The Appellant argues that, although the Philippine government has taken measures to protect women in abusive relationships, they are ineffective. The Appellant essentially bases this argument on the increase in the incidence of reported domestic abuse.

The RAD is not persuaded by the Appellant's argument in this regard. Where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police, civil authority in place and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact that it is not always successful at doing so will not be enough to justify a claim that the victims are unable to avail themselves of protection. The fact that state protection is not perfect does not constitute clear and convincing proof of the state's inability to protect citizens since no state can guarantee the protection of all its citizens at all times.

The RAD has considered the nature of the human rights violation in the context of the adequacy of state protection for gender-based crimes. The RAD also applied the Chairperson's Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution11 in assessing the evidence and in rendering its decision.

The RAD has further considered the profile of the agent of persecution. Although the objective evidence in the record does suggest that in smaller communities, some abusers use their personal contacts to avoid prosecution of gender-related crimes, the RAD notes that there is no evidence in the record and none raised by the Appellant in this appeal that suggests that the Appellant's husband is in a position of power or has close ties to the police or other authorities in the Philippines and that, because of this, state protection would not be forth coming.

Although the incidence of reported crime has risen, the RAD notes that domestic violence is a widespread problem in the Philippines, and there is no evidence which indicates that the incidence of domestic violence in the Philippines is greater than the incidence of domestic violence in other developed countries including North America. Furthermore, the RAD finds that, while the documentary evidence indicates that the incidence of reported crime has increased, it does not provide the context to explain the increase. For instance, the increase may simply be a result of the institution of a broader definition of what constitutes domestic violence, awareness, or, it could be a result of increased and more effective police response to reported incidents of domestic violence.

Notwithstanding the reason for the increase in the incidence of domestic violence, the RAD notes that, according to the US Department of State, Philippines, Country Report on Human Rights Practices for 201412 tendered by the Appellant of the 23,761 cases of domestic violence cases, the police laid nearly 16,000 charges, 869 remain under investigation, 3,752 were settled and 3,402 were referred to other agencies for further investigation. The RAD also notes that "protection orders" which are intended to prevent further acts of violence are accessible to victims of domestic violence. The RAD finds that this is compelling evidence that the authorities in the Philippines take domestic violence seriously and that, if the Appellant were to seek protection, it would be forthcoming.

While it is true that the objective evidence indicates that some victims of domestic violence have experienced some resistance from some police officers in seeking protection, the RAD also notes there is an Ombudsman present in the country to deal with complaints when victims feel they have received unfair treatment at the hands of the authorities.13

The RAD finds that the government has been taking steps to deal with the issue of violence against women and therefore has demonstrated a willingness to deal with the issue. It also appears their efforts have been reasonably effective. While the protection provided by the Philippines is not perfect, it is the finding of the RAD that the protection available is adequate.
Based on the foregoing, the RAD finds adequate state protection is available to the Appellant if she seeks it upon her return to the Philippines.
The RAD finds that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

Pursuant to Section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, the Refugee Appeal Division confirms the decision of the Refugee Protection Division. (signed) "L. Favreau" L.
